messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Dev Patel, an eighty-year-old South Asian American who spent his working life in the Coast Guard, carries a clinical profile that reflects the weight he bears. It was a tide-worn embankment twenty-eight years ago that anchored his mind. He had been securing a heavy mooring line when the tension snapped, and the steel pulley swung backward, striking a young deckhand across the ribs. Dev felt the sickening crack through his own palms before he even turned. He had come to believe that the force of the line, the specific angle of the rocks, and the sudden release of the tide were all tied together, and that if he had simply waited three seconds longer, the deckhand would have walked away unharmed. In the months that followed, Dev noticed his mind splitting into fragments. He could not pull the event forward when he tried deliberately; instead, the memory arrived in disconnected flashes: the wet grip of the rope, the sharp metallic ring, the deckhand’s widened eyes. When it flooded back, it did not feel like a recollection at all. It was completely real, pressing against his skin, filling his lungs with salt air, echoing in his ears. He tried to push the images away, telling himself over and over that the man had recovered, that it did not really happen or was not that bad. He forced himself to speak only of the positive outcomes, to reframe the stumble as a necessary part of the job. Yet a quiet conviction settled in him: there was something wrong with his hands, with his judgment. He was the sort of man who let things slip, the sort of man who caused harm without meaning to. The event had happened to him because of the character he carried. The Coast Guard station became his daily anchor, a working environment of salt-stained docks, iron bulkheads, and whistling winches where he spent his days coordinating vessel movements. He had to be on guard all the time, watching the horizon, listening for the first wail of a siren. When a patrol vessel’s horn cut through the morning, his shoulders would tighten, certain that another accident was already unfolding. He avoided unfamiliar places. He could not assess the ground beneath him, and the unknown space felt uncertain. He took to safe seat seeking, always choosing the aisle or the corner where his back was against a wall and his escape route was clear. Still, he took too many risks on the dock—climbing wet ladders too quickly, walking the narrow gangplanks without hesitation—proving to himself that he was strong, though sometimes his haste brought on bruises, and on occasion, minor harm to others. Now widowed after forty years, Dev still attends weekly Coast Guard gatherings at the coastal maritime hall. His children live across the country, and when they speak of retirement trips, of doctors’ appointments years down the line, of moving closer to grandchildren, Dev listens carefully. But talking about the future makes his chest feel tight; he wonders if he will be the one to fall, to pull a line the wrong way again. His memory still refuses to sit still, and his thoughts are a quiet battle between suppression and relief. He has finally come to therapy after years of carrying this quiet tension, hoping to understand why his own body and mind feel so heavily armed. What frightens him most is not the past itself, but the feeling that his own nature will continue to bring trouble into his days, and that he will never be certain enough to step into the unknown without fear.
